paragraphs.text: Come, let us take up the promise again and carry the subject of paradise through to the end. For if it was an unbearable misfortune that Adam was driven out of paradise, it will be a far greater one if we too are driven out of the memory of paradise. Let us take up the subject, then, not leaving the inquiry to ordinary reasoning, but drawing the solution to the difficulties from holy Scripture itself. For whoever thinks and judges as he pleases deceives himself; but whoever learns the solution to the difficulties from Scripture has truth itself as his teacher. Since, then, many of the faithful are puzzled when they read, and many unbelievers blaspheme out of ignorance, let us take it up as far as our ability allows, so as to give the saints full assurance and the unbelievers a refutation, and let us call on God together with you to supply the truth in abundance. How man was made, how he was formed in body, how a soul created by God was placed in his body, how he had paradise for his dwelling: all this has been sufficiently discussed already, if not as it deserves, at least as far as our ability allowed. Now let us turn our discourse to the matter before us. The whole earth was given to Adam, but paradise was his special dwelling. He was allowed to walk outside paradise too. But what lay outside paradise was not set apart for human habitation; it was for the irrational creatures: the cattle, the four-footed beasts, the wild animals, the reptiles. Paradise was his royal and lordly residence. That is why God brought the animals to Adam, since they lived apart from him. For servants do not always stand beside their master, but only when they are needed. The animals were named and at once sent out, but Adam remained in paradise. Now let us learn to understand this point precisely.

The irrational creatures were permitted to come to Adam, to bow before him and fawn on him. Let me explain what I mean. Just as there were three kinds of trees, for there were trees that nourished him so that he might live, trees that tested him so that he might live well, and a tree that preserved him so that he might live forever, so too three kinds of irrational animals were given to him: one for food (and this was set apart not for him alone but for the whole race), one for food, another for service, and another for delight. For food, the animals that are sacrificed now; for service, horses, camels, donkeys, oxen and the other working animals; for delight, the animals that mimic, and the bright songs of the birds of the air, which charm the ear. For just as the body after toil cannot endure further toil unless it first sheds its fatigue, so the soul that bears the labors of virtue cannot keep up the strain of virtue unless it is refreshed by pleasant sights. When God sees a soul worn out, he refreshes it with pleasant things. This happens among us too. Often a man comes home from the marketplace, his mind flooded with countless sorrows; often he has met with grievous sights and fallen into unbearable misfortunes and losses. When he enters his house he finds refreshment in his little child, and the softness of the child soothes the harshness of his troubles. For when he is downcast, his wife does not come to comfort him, since her comfort would be ill-timed, and no servant dares to console him; so God brings in that unaffected nature which is pardoned because of what it does not know, and through it he soothes the soul worn out by its troubles. If a servant smiles at him, he is thought to be laughing at his master's humiliation; if his wife laughs, she is thought to be insensible to the misfortune; but the child's coaxing is above suspicion because of the innocence of its nature. And often what friends could not achieve with their advice, or wise men with their admonitions, a child has achieved simply by laughing, dispelling the whole misfortune. The soul, at the very height of its grief, sees the child and at first turns away, rejecting the ill-timed comfort; but it is drawn by the child's persistence, and after turning its eyes toward it again and again, its mind is captivated. Then the man takes the child in his arms, lays his grief aside and says, "Let God spare me this one alone, and I care nothing for the rest."

Do you see how God raises up comfort for the soul even from ordinary things? Since, then, Adam was alone in paradise, with no friend, no neighbor, no kinsman, God brought the animals to him for his delight: animals like the mimics we have today, some imitating gestures and others sounds. The ape, for instance, and others like it imitate human gestures; the parrot and other birds imitate the voice. So he had delight from the irrational creatures, some singing and others fawning on him. Now among the many that supplied him with comfort, the serpent was the most intelligent of all the beasts of the earth, as Scripture said: "Now the serpent was the most intelligent of all the beasts that the Lord God had made."

So it was the best mimic among the mimics and the closest among those that fawned on him. Do not judge by how it appears now, when we flee from it and loathe it. It was not so from the beginning. The serpent was a friend, closer to man than any of the creatures that fawned on him. Who, then, made it an enemy? God's sentence: "Cursed are you above all the beasts. I will put enmity between you and the woman." That enmity dissolved the friendship. By friendship I mean not a rational one but an irrational recognition. Just as a dog today shows a semblance of friendship, not by reason but by natural impulse, so the serpent fawned on man. Since it was on such intimate terms with him, the devil saw it as a suitable instrument. Seeing that Adam delighted in the serpent, and that the serpent fawned on him and imitated many human things, the craftsman of evil devised what those who weave plots do when they corrupt people through those close to them. For no one prevails through strangers, only through intimates, as the Savior said: "A man's enemies will be those of his own household." So he speaks through the serpent, giving Adam a false impression. I urge you, beloved, not to pay casual attention to what is said. This is no ordinary question. Many ask how the serpent spoke: was it with a human voice, or with a serpent's hiss, and Eve understood it? Before the transgression Adam was filled with wisdom, understanding and prophecy. Consider how much wisdom he had: one man, without a teacher, instructed by no human being, was able to give names to all the birds, the animals, the creeping beasts, in short to everything. Picture in your mind all the species and kinds. To put it briefly, he gave so many names that today, with all our experience, we cannot repeat them. So when God brought the animals to the man, since he was wise and had the Spirit of God, he saw the particular character of each. He therefore paid attention to the serpent as being more intelligent, as having perception, as understanding movements from gestures. With Adam disposed in this way, the devil took note both of the serpent's intelligence and of Adam's preconception, for Adam regarded the serpent as clever. So he speaks through it, so that Adam would suppose that the serpent, being intelligent, had even managed to imitate the human voice. So the serpent approaches. Nowhere does Scripture say that the devil spoke in the serpent; Moses simply related the story. Pay close attention, I beg you. Paul, the second man to be in paradise, did not alter the wording either, but says: "I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ. But I am afraid that, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning…" And he did not say "the devil." He was a faithful guardian of the Scriptures, a servant of the Scriptures, a teacher of the Scriptures, an interpreter of the Scriptures. He did not want to alter the wording, lest he disturb the order of the Scriptures, but he resolved the difficulty through the sense. "I am afraid," he says, "that, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your thoughts may be corrupted." "So": how? Surely Paul was not afraid that the serpent would come again and deceive people? No, he is saying: "I know that the serpent itself does not appear, but the one who worked in it does." Paul, then, as a faithful servant and guardian of the holy Scriptures, did not change the wording, but brought the sense to light. But the Master of things ancient, present and to come himself made the difficulty plain, so that no one would lay the sin on the serpent, but on the one who worked through it. For when the Jews said to him, "We are from God," Christ said to them: "If you were from God, you would do the works and the will of God; but as it is, you are of your father the devil." He named the devil and immediately brought in the story: "He was a murderer of men from the beginning." The servant interpreted as a servant; the Master taught as Master: he pointed out the one who killed Adam. He did not simply say "he was a murderer," but "a murderer of men," for he did not destroy one man only, but through him every human being. "And he did not stand in the truth," he says, "because he is a liar."

See how he explained both that he is the devil and that he is a liar. And how did he lie? The serpent said to the woman: "Why is it that God told you not to eat from every tree?" Do you see the liar? God said: "From every tree you shall eat, but from one you shall not eat." The liar says: "Why did God tell you not to eat from every tree?" Can Christ's word lie? "He is a liar." And he lied, and cunningly too. For when someone wants to do something malicious, he pretends ignorance for the purpose, so as to introduce his mischief without arousing suspicion, as if to say: "I don't know; there's no scheme; I came in all innocence, I know nothing." Have you not met many such people? Do we not know the ways of the deceitful? Do they not stitch together such schemes while pretending ignorance? So too the devil: "Why is it," he says, "that God told you…", as if to say, "I misheard, I didn't hear properly", "…not to eat from every tree?" The woman, thinking it was ignorance, corrects his words. "That is not what he said," she says. "God did not say not to eat from every tree; he allowed every tree, but forbade one. For he told us: 'You shall not eat, lest you die.'" He seemed to be learning what he had not known, so he was not suspected of scheming, and he says to her: "You will not surely die." Look, another lie. For when God had said, "On the day you eat, you shall surely die," the devil says, "You will not die." That was his second lie.

"For God knew," he says, "that on the day you eat, you will be like gods." Look, a third lie. See the devil's scheming wickedness. Already he is preparing to sow error in the world. And since he was planning, as I said before, to raise up polytheism in the world, he anticipated it as though in passing, and sowed in the woman's ears the impression that there are many gods. But while the craftsman of evil thus sowed the notion of gods in advance, God, foreseeing it, arranged that the coming error [?] should not be spoken by a human mouth, so that the first rational voice would not speak of gods; rather, the first mouth to do so was a serpent's, so that every mouth that speaks of idols might be likened to that mouth. I know that you forgive my manner of speaking and lay hold of the holy meanings of the Scriptures. So let no one be occupied with the polish of the words, but with the force of the thoughts. "For God knew," he says, "that on the day you eat, you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." Many say, especially the followers of the God-hated Porphyry, who wrote against the Christians and turned many away from divine doctrine; they say: "Why did God forbid the knowledge of good and evil? Granted, he forbade evil; but why good as well? For by saying, 'Do not eat from the tree of knowing good and evil,' he prevents him from knowing evil. Why good as well?" Wickedness always plots against itself and gives a handle against itself. God did not forbid the knowledge of good, for Adam had it even before he ate. For if he had no knowledge, how did he recognize the woman? How could he explain her nature: "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh"? And how did he prophesy what was to come: "She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her husband. For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother," and the rest? He knew so much, and did not know the good? He knew God, he kept God's commands, he had knowledge, he gave so many names. How could he not have had knowledge of the good? What, then, does it mean? God does not forbid the knowledge of the good; rather, he wills that knowledge of evil should not be joined to the good. I refute this impious sophistry from the Scriptures. Paul says: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons." He did not forbid both; he sanctified the holy and rejected the accursed and profane. So too the Savior: "You cannot serve God and mammon"; in the same way it is impossible to serve both God and a demon. In this way God forbade him to acquire knowledge of evil, so that the knowledge of evil would not be mixed with the good.

So now let us pay attention here. Why was it called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil at all? It did not have such a nature; rather, it gave rise to such an event. I am speaking of the idiom of the Scriptures. Here is what I mean. In the wilderness a spring of water was called "the water of dispute": "I tested you at the water of dispute." Did the water have such a nature that it drove the people to dispute? Then why did Moses not dispute with God when he drank? Just as the water was called the water of dispute, not because it had such a nature but because of what happened at it — since the people disputed there, it was called the water of dispute — so again, Jacob saw God, as far as a human being can see him, and he calls the name of the place "Form of God." The place did not have the form of God or the shape of God, but because the vision came to him there, he named the place after the event. Another place was called "Peace of God." When an angel appeared to Gideon, he was afraid and said: "Woe is me, woe is me, I shall die, for I have seen an angel of God." The angel said to him: "Peace be with you; do not be afraid." And Gideon, it says, built an altar and called it "Peace of God." Just as the altar, the place of sacrifice, did not itself possess peace but was a symbol of the peace that had come about and been given, and just as the water did not possess dispute but was so called because of what happened at it, so too the tree did not possess knowledge. It was so named because everyone who sins comes to know what he has sinned in. Let me put it another way, again with an illustration. Sometimes when we travel we pass through places plagued by robbers, and people usually say: "These places are frightening." Does the place itself contain fear? Or do they say it because of the robbers who lurk in that place? In the same way, that tree did not have a nature that produced a deadly knowledge; it took its name from the tragedy that befell Adam over it. I will settle the matter briefly, for divine Scripture is never at a loss. Today we have an altar in which the faithful partake. Does the offering itself possess salvation by nature, or through the glory invoked upon it? You have a guarantee from the present; do not be in doubt about what happened before. There, a food that brought death; here, a food that gives life. If this food saves by nature and not by grace, then that one also kills by nature and not through transgression. I will show you another deadly food outside paradise: I mean idolatry. Why did the martyrs refuse to eat meat? Why were they afraid to eat? If they had eaten, would they have died? Not at all. But because the memory of the idols had been named over it, they shunned not the eating but the invocation of the abominable ones. So the tree was "of the knowledge of evil and good," not because it imparted knowledge, but because it taught him through the transgression. For experience always teaches the foolish that transgressing is evil. Once more the question will be resolved by another route — not because the first answers are weak, but because the grace of God is rich. Let no one think that I bring in many interpretations because the earlier ones are weak. The grace of God is rich, and it supplies us from its own treasures, if we are worthy. Pay attention, then. The martyrs refused to eat food sacrificed to idols and truly shunned eating it, just as Adam would have been saved if he had shunned the tree. That it is not knowing good and evil that is hateful, the truth makes plain. For I ask: does God, who does not do evil, know it or not? Who dares to say that he does not know? Knowledge is not action. When Paul says, "Flee fornication," did he not know what fornication was? Did the man who shuns adultery not know what adultery was? Yet knowledge did not condemn him. And God himself knows all our deeds, listing them and saying: "Out of the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, perjuries, licentiousness, envy, greed. These are what defile a person." Do God and the apostle say these things in ignorance or with knowledge? So knowledge brings no disgrace on Adam. It was not knowledge that harmed him, but transgression. I would like to ask him: what good or evil did he learn from the tree? After eating, did he know what murder is? There was as yet no one who punished. Adultery was unknown, for there were not yet any marriages; there were no fornications; there was no robbery, for there were not yet rich and poor; there were no slanders and false testimonies. What evil, then, did he come to know, except only this: that it was good to obey God and evil to disobey God? I will quote a common, everyday saying, and let no one condemn it as too bold. We often say to wrongdoers, threatening them with correction: "I'll make you learn to mend your ways." Does the speaker mean learning in the sense of knowledge? So the "knowledge" comes from the experience of misfortune. It taught him, once he had transgressed, to know how many good things he had been joined to.

Pay careful attention, then. Even if this was said before, the subject draws the discourse along. God, who had given all things, was invisible; the one who had received all things from God was visible. The receiver was seen; the giver was not seen. Man was alone, with the irrational creatures around him. He had no one over his head. God set a law for him: the tree in the middle as a reminder, so that, having received dominion, he would not forget. For example, he would go about gathering fruit with his wife. He would come near the tree and say: "Let us not touch this tree, for God gave a command about it." So the visible thing was a reminder of the invisible one, just as happens even now. Think how many rulers there are throughout the whole earth. Since the emperor is not present to everyone, the emperor's image has to be present in law courts, in marketplaces, in assemblies, in theaters. In every place where a ruler acts it has to be present, so that what is done may be valid. The emperor, being a man, cannot be present everywhere; and again, it is impossible for God to appear to human beings as God. So he gave the tree as the image of his sovereignty, reminding Adam that he had received dominion over all things: "Know the one who gave you authority." And so that you may learn how the tree reminded them: when the serpent wanted to deceive the woman, he said to her, "Why did God say that you should not eat from every tree?" The woman had not forgotten the law; she even corrects his ignorance and says: "God did not say that. We may eat from every tree; but of this tree God said, 'Do not eat from it, and do not touch it.'" See the precision. God did not say, "Do not touch." Touching carried no danger. But they, possessing godly understanding and enjoying everything else, decided among themselves: "God told us not to taste of the tree, but we will not even touch it." That is how much the woman cared about keeping God's commandment. So the tree stood in the middle, and through it he deceived them. Hear something strange. As his instrument of deception he used something implanted in man himself. For when God formed man, along with the rest of his knowledge he placed in him a longing for God. So when the serpent saw the flame of that longing in them, he says: "You will be like gods. Now, as human beings, you cannot always be with God. If you become like gods, you will always be with him." He did not say to them, "If you eat, you will become God's enemies." So the desire for equality with God deceives the woman, and she does not deceive the man but persuades him. Paul bears witness to this when he says: "Adam was not deceived." Then why was he condemned? See how serious it is. The woman was deceived and ate; after eating she persuades her husband as well, so that she would not be ruined alone. She persuaded him; she did not deceive him — as often happens even now. A man knows the faith, loves the law, is zealous for orthodoxy, and yet is persuaded by his wife not to show his zeal — not because he is ignorant of the truth, but because he gives in to his spouse. Many have supposed that Adam took the fruit from the woman in ignorance, not knowing where she had brought it from. But he has no defense, for God convicts him, saying to him: "Because you listened to the voice of your wife." He did not say, "Because you took it from your wife" — and Adam could indeed have said, "I was unaware; I did not know where she had brought the fruit from." The man is charged not with having been deceived, but with having been enticed. Now let us come to the courtroom. Let us look at the first records of that holy, impartial and merciful trial, written in immortal letters, whose memory, appearance and brilliance not even all the ages can erase. Pay attention, then. Adam heard, it says, the voice of the Lord walking in paradise in the afternoon. He perceived him from the sound and from habit. Could God be made known by a footfall? He appeared not as he was, but as he wished. Blessed be the God of the saints, who visited Adam then in the afternoon, and now on the cross in the afternoon. For the Savior endured his passion during the very hours that Adam spent between eating, transgressing and being judged: from the sixth hour to the ninth. He ate at the sixth hour — that is the rule of nature; after the sixth he hid; in the afternoon God came to him. Adam desired to become God, but he desired the impossible; Christ fulfilled his desire. "You desired to become what you could not; I desire to become man, which I can." For God balanced his deception with its counterpart. "You desired what is above you; I take on what is below me. You desired equality with God; I become equal with man." That is why Paul too says: "And being found in appearance as a man." "You desired to become God, and I was not angry at that — for I want you to long for equality with God. My anger is that you tried to seize that dignity against your Master's will. You desired to become God and could not; I become man and make the impossible possible." That he came to this out of desire, he himself testifies, when he was eating the Passover — he who feeds all, eating with those he feeds, a table set before him who feeds everything under heaven. He says to the apostles: "With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you." "Did I begrudge you equality with God? You tried to seize what is mine and could not; I take what is yours, and can." Pay attention. He came down in the afternoon and says: "Adam, where are you?"

Those events and these are sisters, for both belong to one God. Was it someone else who came to the passion, and not the one who came down in paradise? Adam hid; he became aware after eating. "For their eyes were opened," it says, "and they knew that they were naked." Since the devil had said, "On the day you eat, your eyes will be opened," someone says, "Look, Satan told the truth." It is fitting to say with Paul: "For we are not ignorant of his designs." The saints know the devil's schemes. See his malice. How did the devil know that after eating their eyes would be opened? Were they blind? Scripture says, before they ate from the tree: "The woman saw the tree." So she was not blind. "The woman saw that the tree was beautiful to look at." First she saw, and then she ate. How then were their eyes opened? Pay attention, I beg you. Here is the question. The devil had come from a fall, that is, from a transgression; and he knew what he, the transgressor, had suffered, and what those who transgress suffer. This experience is common to all. Even today, when we sin, we sin as though blind; and once we have sinned, then we see what we have done. For example, if someone is accused — "Why did you do this?" — he pleads that he could not help it: "Truly, I did not see what I was doing." Not that he was blind, but in sin reason is crippled; it becomes wholly absorbed in the act and is blinded while acting. Afterwards he sees with his conscience what he has done. Let me give a hypothetical case. Someone goes into a house to rob it, and he goes in like a blind man. He takes no account of who might meet him or seize him, of the fear of the judges, of the danger hanging over him, for he is blinded by his sickness. Once he has gone in, once he has taken, once he has come out with his loot, though no one is there, he is filled with fear. He realizes what he has done and reckons that if there is an inquiry, they will know whose work it is. What he did not reckon with while acting, he reckons with after the act. Or take the adulterer, who throws himself into another man's fire: he goes in without reckoning that there are laws, courts, accusations, sharpened swords. But once he has done it, he is afraid; he suspects the slave-boy, the slave-girl, the neighbor, the relative. What he did not see while doing it, he sees after the deed. Again, someone advises another to keep away from wickedness. If he disobeys, common usage says of him: "I told him many times and he didn't hear" — not that he literally did not hear. Then, after giving him a beating, he says, "I'm teaching you to hear" — not that he gives him the faculty of hearing, but that the blow corrects his obstinacy and brings him to understanding. So too the prophet: "The discipline of the Lord opens my ears." Since, then, the devil fell — for I have not forgotten my subject — he knew where he was after falling, and then he became aware of what he had done. He learned from what he suffered, and so he says: "If you eat, your eyes will be opened" — that is, as mine were. "I know what I suffered once I transgressed; I came to know what I suffered; I came to know what I had lost." Then they ate, and their eyes were opened, and they saw that they were naked. Before this they were naked and were not ashamed. They were stripped of immortality, the robe of glory was taken from them, the body was laid bare, and from then on it was clay. At once the invention of crafts springs up. Adam's first craft was sewing. Before any other craft, he took fig leaves and sewed them. Who taught him? Who trained him? He had received understanding from God once and for all; he was the image of God — and do you doubt his knowledge? Consider for yourself: how did man first make a plough? Who showed him how to shape the wood, fit the iron into the middle, bind it tight, and put a yoke on the oxen? How did woman discover the craft of weaving — to take the fleece, wash it, card it, spin it, draw out what is joined and join again what is split? Where does this come from? Who taught embroiderers the art of embroidery? The loom stands; one thread is passed through; it is not the hand that works but reason that works; reason produces the figures. The craftsman does not lay his hands on them, yet the principle of the craft shapes the garment, and the craftsman's intention rises up in visible figures. The embroiderer does not move his hand, and yet he raises up forms. So when you hear that God works, do you think he works by moving a hand? And if you inquire into every craft and every invention and ask, "How did they think of this or that?", then by remembering the first words, "Let us make man according to our image," you have the solution to the problem. An image of God, and not understand? An image of God, and not imitate the Master? He sewed fig leaves.

Let those who allegorize be put to shame, who say that paradise is in heaven and is spiritual. What would a fig tree be doing in heaven? But suppose paradise is in heaven. Where do the rivers come from? Is it not from the earth? If paradise is above, then clearly the rivers too flow from above. But did Scripture say, "A river comes down from Eden"? Yet here is their clever argument; the allegorists laugh at us: "For God clothed them," it says, "with garments of skin." Did he slaughter oxen or sheep, open a tannery and practice the tanner's trade? We say: he brought forth the whole animal without intercourse, without mating. He made what did not exist — could he not make part of what exists? Then they press their point: "But God never makes part of an animal; God makes nothing incomplete." Such a person hears "skin" and asks where it came from. Well then, I too hear of blood in Egypt, and I ask where he got it from when he turned the Nile into blood, and what animals he slaughtered. The river became blood, and no animal was slaughtered. Two skins came into being, and he asks from what animals they came. So there too: skin without an animal. Follow the train of thought, even if my voice is tired, and you are too. But so that the discourse is not cut short, I will say a few things quietly and then bring it to a close. He sewed fig leaves. If only the heretics had learned this craft! Adam, after transgressing, learned to sew; the heretics, after going astray, learned to tear. Adam, after transgressing, sewed in order to cover his shame; the heretics, after coming to faith, tear in order to lay bare the holy things. We often hear what happened at the cross and are amazed that soldiers took Christ's garments and divided them, and at once our mind says: "Great is God's patience, that no thunderbolt came down, no sword came down! The Holy One was insulted, and those profane hands were not cut off?" Are you amazed that those soldiers dared to divide the garments? Be amazed that these men have torn apart the garment of the church. The soldiers saw that Christ's tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from the top, and they spared the garment. But the heretics have torn, divided and cut to pieces the clothing of Christ, the robe of the church. But let us return to our subject. He sewed fig leaves. They heard God walking, as far as one can hear him; they heard and hid. Our nature is honest: even if we are sinners ten thousand times over, our conscience is free. Sometimes the face is shameless and the conscience convicts; sometimes the tongue says, "What sin have I committed?" and the conscience convicts from within. Adam and his wife were utterly simple and guileless; they confessed openly. God says, "Where are you?" Many have interpreted this piously. But we must attend to precision. I accept their interpretations, since they are pious, and I say what I say because it is true. "Adam, where are you?" — Where have you come from? Where have you come down to? From what glory have you fallen? Truly I accept this idea as pious, for it has both propriety and compassion. But I am looking for the train of thought. "Adam, where are you?" God asks. As the one who formed him, he knew the nature of what he had formed: that everyone who has sinned loses his boldness, and that the mouths of sinners are sewn shut. He noticed that Adam had fled because he had lost his boldness. A slave is most anxious when he realizes that his master has found out what happened. As long as the master does not know, he comforts himself that he may escape notice. Adam fled as one found out; God pretended not to know, in order to dispel his fear — just as we say about a friend: "I acted as though I didn't know, so as not to hurt him." Such things often happen among us. And if such things happen among us, how much more with God, who loves humankind! "Adam, where are you?" stands for "I do not know." Then, since God was pretending not to know, that honest and free soul did not hide anything: "I heard your voice and was afraid, because I am naked, and I hid." Why were you afraid? Why did you hide? "I was afraid because of the transgression; I hid because of my nakedness." Truly, one could weep at the words of the transgressor. "I heard your voice" — that beloved voice, that voice which gave me all things, that voice which gave me good things and provided for me. "I heard your voice. I realized what kind of voice I had spat upon, what kind of voice I had despised. And I was afraid, having broken the command of such a Master; and I hid, because I am naked." Then God continues to encourage him: "Who told you that you are naked, unless you have eaten from the tree from which alone I commanded you not to eat?" — that is, "unless you have indeed done what I forbade." See how he asks as if he did not know: "unless you have eaten from that tree from which I commanded you not to eat." And see God's love for humanity: "Who told you?" He draws out the conversation so as to dispel Adam's fear and awaken his confidence. For Adam saw that there was nothing harsh, nothing severe, no insult, no blows. Everyday life teaches you this. When a slave who has done wrong comes before his master, he takes either courage or fear from the very first words. If the master starts to rage and calls him a thief and a cheat and worthy of ten thousand deaths, he goes to pieces; but if he hears him reproach him, "You wretch, how did this happen to you? Why did you do wrong?", he is at once heartened and takes courage for the moment. For the master is not punishing him as a master but admonishing him as a teacher. So too God: "Who told you that you are naked, unless you have eaten from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?" "Did I forbid you many things? I forbade only one, and not out of hatred but out of care for you." "Who told you that you are naked?" Adam did not shamelessly say, "I didn't know." What then? "The woman you gave me — she gave it to me, and I ate" — that is, "the one given to me as a helper. For I heard you say, when I had been formed and she not yet: 'Let us make him a helper like himself.' The one you gave me, she gave it to me." He did not say, "She deceived me"; he did not lie. "She gave it to me, and I ate."

Then God says: "Should you have believed a woman and not me? Is the woman more trustworthy than I am? I gave you good things and honored you with deeds; she lured you with words." And notice: when a judge accepts the defense of the person on trial and questions him no further, but moves on to someone else, the accused at once takes heart and says, "For now, my examination is over." In the same way God moves on from Adam to relieve his fear, and says to the woman: "What is this you have done?" She says: "The serpent deceived me, and I ate." Because she told the whole truth, he does not insult the defense of truth but leaves it unexamined. He did not say: "And was that one, that is, the serpent, believed over me? He promised you equality with God and brought about death instead." He does not pass judgment at once. Rather, he spared her as the weaker vessel, and he moves on to the serpent, to persuade both him and her that he is proceeding against the one who was to blame. And he says: "Because you have done this." Do you see what a wonderful judge he is? He questions those who were deceived; he does not question the deceiver. He does not say to him, "What have you done?" but "Because you have done this." It is in this sense that David says: "The ungodly will not rise up in judgment": not that they will not be raised, but that they will not be examined. "Because you have done this." The threat against the serpent lightened the blows dealt to those who had been deceived. For, as the reasoning goes, had God not laid the whole blame on him, he would not have condemned him without examination. "Because you have done this, cursed are you above all the wild beasts of the earth. On your breast and belly you shall go." Because you have done this, because you deceived a heart and persuaded a belly to touch food, on your breast and belly you shall go. God does not now decree that it shall go on its belly as though it had used feet before. Rather, it was standing upright when it spoke with the woman, for there was no other way for it to hold a conversation with Eve. The very posture in which it held the conversation by which it deceived Eve is what he punishes by making it go on its breast, and he casts it out of its upright gait. For even if it had been made without feet from the beginning, it would raise itself up on the coils of certain swift windings beneath it and ride along with its chest stretched out. That is why even now a serpent, when it is enraged, often rears itself up and runs along winding in coils. But after going forward just far enough to show the memory of its old gait, it is thrown down again by the law of the sentence. "And earth you shall eat all the days of your life. I will put enmity between you and the woman." What does "earth you shall eat" mean? Eat what you brought Adam to become. For he is about to hear: "Earth you are, and to earth you shall return." "I will put enmity between you and the woman." Since you deceived her as a friend, you are cast out as an enemy. That word became a law. Pay attention, then. "Earth you shall eat all the days of your life." Look: he is not saying of the serpent, "The earth will be your food." For snakes do not always eat earth. They also feed on meat, feast on fruit, take seeds and hunt for herbs. Rather, by saying "earth you shall eat," he means this: "You will wear away the earth," he says, "by rubbing along it."

But some people say: if it was the devil who deceived, why did the serpent receive the curse? God scourges the invisible demon with an invisible blow, and he subjects the visible instrument to a visible punishment. Why? Just as God, who is invisible, gave the tree as a visible reminder, so the devil, who is invisible, speaks to human beings through the serpent. So God puts the serpent under a curse. Then, whatever harm someone has suffered from the devil, he always sees the serpent crawling along, the creature that once stood upright, and takes it as a reminder: if the servant of wickedness is punished like this, how much more the one who did the deed himself? Pay attention, then. You find something akin to this in the Gospel. In the visible serpent God condemned the one who spoke along with the visible creature. In the same way, in the Gospel, when the demons begged Christ not to send them into the abyss, they said, "Allow us to go into the pigs." He allowed them to go in, so that he might drown the invisible beings together with the visible bodies. "You shall eat earth." "I will put enmity between you and the woman." He turned friendship into enmity, and his word became law. People are eager to tame other wild animals, but when someone sees a snake, he recoils. For the decree still stands: "I will put enmity between you." If he sees one in the house, he wants to kill it; if he sees one on the road, he is wild to kill it. The ancient word goads him on. He may give the snake countless blows, but if he sees that its head has not been wounded, he immediately urges whoever is standing by: "You haven't hit the snake's head. Strike at the head!" For God said, "He will watch for your head, and you will watch for his heel." What does this mean? God does not say, "I will make man refrain from striking the other members of your body and punish only the head." A man strikes the serpent on every part of it, punishing the whole wherever he hits. And what the Master said to the serpent, "You will watch for his heel," does not declare that serpents have been given access only to the heel. They sometimes attack people even while they sleep; they often seize on the belly and inject their venom; they bite the hands and the other members. In short, no human limb that comes in their way remains unharmed. Rather, the meaning of the sentence is this: "No longer," he says, "will the serpent plot openly against man. You will stay inside and be so afraid of human beings that you hide yourself in holes and barely peep out of crevices, in fear, watching only for people to pass by so that you can come out without danger. But man," he says, "will walk about without fear, while your head is kept in holes, like a hidden enemy's, no longer speaking to him as to a friend."

But since time presses, let us also finish our discourse. God questioned the woman who had been deceived, and then he moves on to the deceiver. So the sentence began from the root, from the deceiver. Then he came to the one who had been deceived and threatens her. The first word to the serpent was "Cursed." "And God said to the woman: I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning." He does not curse her so that she would not bear children, since he had already given his blessing. For when he formed them, Scripture says, "And God blessed them, saying, Increase and multiply, and fill the earth." And Paul says, "The gifts of God are irrevocable." So he does not curse those whom he has blessed. What does he do, then? He applies a strange remedy to the wound: sorrow and groaning. It has the form of a sentence that strikes, but it promises release from the fault. "I will greatly multiply," he says, "your sorrows and your groaning." These are remedies of repentance. Pay attention. Physicians use the same medicine both to sting and to heal; the same incision, the same scalpel, and the same pain that comes with the cut bring about health. In the same way God gives the woman who sinned two provisions for repentance, sorrow and groaning. What good does sorrow do? Hear Paul when he says, "For godly sorrow produces a repentance that leads to salvation and brings no regret." And what does groaning accomplish? Hear Isaiah: "When you turn back and groan, then you will be saved." "I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning." Sorrow disfigures the outward face and makes it gloomy. When the heart rejoices, the face blooms; when the heart is in sorrow, the face is downcast. The eye saw the tree, and the mind reckoned on becoming equal to God. So God gives groaning to the heart and sorrow to the face, so that she might be punished through the very things by which she sinned. This punishment, or rather this salvation, was also meant to persuade the woman that he had not gone back on the ancient blessing. For having said to them, "Fill the earth," he now says, "In sorrows you shall bear children." "I do not take away childbearing, for I have blessed once and for all; but you will suffer pain, in toil and in turmoil." That sorrow is the heaviest of all. The Savior bears witness to it: "A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow." She grieves in giving birth, and she worries in bringing up the child. When the child comes of age, she worries that he may turn out foolish; if he goes abroad, she worries that he may die, or fall ill, or suffer pain. The man does not have this. Even if the father worries, it is not as the mother does. He consoles himself, saying, "He is a man, he knows how to look after himself," and stops worrying. Why? Because he was not the one who heard, "In sorrows you shall bear children." It is a strange kind of sentence. Experience bears witness. When labor pains seize a woman, not even in those very pains does she renounce her husband. She does not say, "If only there were no marriage! If only there were no childbearing!" God does not let her hate her husband even after this experience. She knows what she suffered and what she endured, and still she loves her husband. That is why it says: "In sorrows you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you." "Since you have just now ruled badly, and he became a slave to your choice, I undo that order. Let the one who was not deceived be master." That is why Paul says, "I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to have authority over a man." For in paradise she taught first, and taught badly. "Nor to have authority over a man": for she exercised authority badly. So it is in this sense that Paul urges that a woman should not teach, because of what happened in paradise. So that we may not seem to be inventing clever arguments, hear him yourself: "I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to have authority over a man." And to show that this is because of those first events, he adds: "For Adam was not deceived, but the woman was deceived and fell into transgression."

What then? Has womankind been placed under condemnation, to remain in sorrows, with the bond never loosed? Christ came, the one who looses the bond. The Mother of the Lord came forward to plead on behalf of her sex, the holy virgin in place of the virgin, for Eve too was a virgin when she sinned. She loosed the sorrow and groaning of the condemned woman. When someone is summoned to the palace, he is eager to honor his own people and, if they are in distress, to set them free. In the same way the holy virgin, summoned to the palace to serve the divine birth and entering into strange birth pangs, asks this as her first favor, or rather receives it. It was not fitting for a condemned woman to give birth to the one who is free of guilt, so he comes who first looses Eve's sorrow through joy. The angel comes and says to the virgin, "Rejoice, favored one." So by the word "Rejoice" he looses the bond of sorrow. "Rejoice": the one who looses sorrow has come. "Rejoice, favored one," since until now you were under a curse. Here pay attention to the grace of God: "Rejoice, favored one; the Lord is with you." With Eve was the serpent, and with it sorrow; rejoice, for with you is God. And see how the angel's words set out the whole saving plan of Christ. "Rejoice, favored one." Since Eve received a double curse, sorrow and groaning in labor, he brings in the birth that undoes that birth: "Behold, you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. For he will save his people from their sins." The fruit that springs from you looses the sins of your forefathers. So the situation has been reversed. To this day those who hear about Eve pity her: "Alas for the wretched woman, what glory she fell from! Alas for the wretched woman, what she suffered!" Mary every day hears herself called "blessed" by everyone, since indeed she was filled with the Holy Spirit. And hear what this virgin says when she prophesies: "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has looked on the lowliness of his handmaid; for from now on all generations will call me blessed." To show that she bears the person of Eve, who until now had been reviled, she says, "From now on all generations will call me blessed." "And what good does it do her," someone asks, "if she does not hear it?" But she certainly does hear it, since she is in a place of light, in the land of the living, she who is the mother of salvation, the fountain of the perceptible light: perceptible because of the flesh, and spiritual because of the divinity. So she is called blessed for all time. But she was also called blessed while she still lived in the flesh, for she heard the blessing while she was still in the flesh. Eve first saw and then tasted of the tree; Mary first spoke and then heard the blessing. For when the Savior was teaching, a woman raised her voice from the crowd and said to him in the hearing of all, "Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that you sucked." Then God completed the sentence upon Adam, or rather the healing remedy of repentance, and says: "Because you listened to your wife's voice and ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the ground in your works." Once again the one who had been blessed does not receive the curse; the ground does. One sinned, and another is struck. So it was with Eve's curse, or rather her rebuke, for it was not a curse but a correction. Eve's rebuke, "In sorrows you shall bear" (and indeed every woman gives birth in sorrows), has remained until now, and so has Adam's: "Cursed is the ground in your works." Our works are lawless, and the ground is scourged. We sin, and the ground receives the curse. God spares his creature as a well-born child and strikes the ground as he would the child's tutor. "Cursed is the ground in your works." Do not look to nature, but to the grace of God. He did not say simply, "Cursed is the ground," for then it would have remained cursed and borne no fruit. When he said to the fig tree, "May no fruit ever come from you again," it withered, and the ground would have fared the same. Instead he says, "in your works." When I sin, the ground is struck; when I do well, he blesses it. And see the wonder of it. When God created the earth, the sea, the birds, the creeping things, the wild beasts, and man, he blessed them all. The fruits he did not bless, for he knew that this punishment was being reserved for the earth: when people sin it would suffer barrenness, and when they act justly it would yield abundance. He did not bless the fruits, for a gift once given could not be revoked. "Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you." "You despised great things," he says, "so be struck by small ones." See how the chastisements are measured: a thorn cannot kill, but it can draw blood. "And you shall eat of the earth in sorrows." She gives birth in sorrows; you must eat in sorrows. For the ancient sentence remains until now. Look for me at a rich man, a poor man, a ruler, a great man, and see whether you can find a life free of sorrow or care. Why? Because of the words "In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread." You were not willing to eat in ease; eat in sweat. He does not punish him with famine, but subjects him to penalty and toil. So you, the believer, consider this: if Adam does not eat bread without sweat, how could we receive the kingdom of heaven without labors and sweat? "Until," he says, "you return to the earth from which you were taken." What a sentence! What a fear, full of love for mankind! What a sentence, full of the promise of recall! He had not yet banished him, and already he called him back; he had not yet cast him out, and already he took him back. "Until you return to the earth from which you were taken." He did not say, "until you are annihilated, until you are dissolved," but "until you return to the earth from which you were taken," so that you might set before yourself the hope of the resurrection. "I am sending you back to where I took you from; as I took you then, I can take you again." "For earth you are, and to earth you shall depart." Not "you will be annihilated," but "you will depart." Some have interpreted "you will depart" as "you will come back." So then, as far as lay within our power, by the provision of the Holy Spirit we have gone through paradise with you. We have read the royal records; we have seen the freedom granted to the guilty and the love for mankind shown by the judge. Through that love may we also receive salvation from Christ, so that we may also enjoy those heavenly and eternal good things, in Christ Jesus our Lord; for to him belong the glory and the might, now and always, and to the ages of ages. Amen.
